quote: Misuse of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Tools: any suspected misuse of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) will be dealt with under this policy.

In most instances misuse of GenAI would fall under the definition of plagiarism (either through failing to appropriately reference sources (i.e. GenAI) or presenting work that is not student’s own as if it were) but could also fall under the definition of dishonest practice where appropriate.
The relevant Discipline Committee will follow Table 9.2 when determining an outcome for forms of Contract Cheating and inappropriate use of GenAI tools (as listed above):
Inappropriate and unethical usage of Large Language Modules (LLMs) and any artificial intelligence technology.

This applies to students who have previously been cited for Contract Cheating and inappropriate use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools, regardless of when the previous offence occurred.

The University may allow reassessment for less severe offences but will not permit for major offences of contract cheating or and inappropriate use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools.
the use of material produced by generative artificial intelligence (GAI) without the specific permission of the tutor/lecturer
where permission to use GAI has been granted, the use of material produced by GAI must be referenced or acknowledged
the use of material produced by paraphrasing tools

The permitted use of AI for a particular assessment or learning activity should be explicitly outlined by Module Coordinators or Supervisors and may differ between modules or contexts according to the University of Stirling’s AI Assessment Scale.
Submission of any form of assessment, which the student has not individually created or written, as the content wholly or substantially originates from output of an artificial intelligence tool.
When part of an assessment originates from an artificial tool without appropriate acknowledgement.
Where an artificial intelligence tool has been used in a manner contrary to the instructions of the particular assessment.
Making false or misleading statements as to the extent to which, and how, artificial intelligence tools were used in an assessment.
Unauthorised notes or information resources in any form, including AI tools.
It is noted that the use of AI tools to paraphrase other students’ work is strictly prohibited as it constitutes a case of collusion.
such a use of AI proofreading tools beyond assistive purposes is also prohibited, unless tasks allow their use for the purposes of formation of ideas or concepts.
Secure and always protect their work, including from unsolicited capture for AI training purposes by online AI providers.
use of most external AI tools for rephrasing students’ own material to avoid selfplagiarism entails the risk of student's own work being used to train future generations of AI services

Students are still required to use AI appropriately according to the University Policy on the use of AI, and to adhere to standards of academic integrity; this includes transparent acknowledgement of AI used.

Users should be aware of the current technical limitations of AI, including but not limited to: generation of inaccurate or fabricated information, lack of source transparency, and reproduction of unintended and potentially harmful biases embedded in training data.
Inappropriate quoting from sources, including artificial intelligence tools, whether or not referenced in-text and/or in the bibliography
unauthorised and / or unacknowledged use of artificial intelligence tools to generate content for assessment purposes
using such technology without explicit permission from relevant academic staff and / or not acknowledging use of such technology when its use is permitted.
unauthorised and / or unacknowledged use of paraphrasing or translation software to, for example, disguise plagiarism, collusion, contract cheating or other academic integrity breach.
It is noted that the UCD Plagiarism Tariff is not appropriate for guiding penalties in relation to other categories of academic misconduct, such as the unauthorised use of generative AI.

Plagiarism through the use of artificial intelligence tools is defined as the unauthorised or unacknowledged use of artificial intelligence tools to generate content for work submitted for assessment.
Traditional plagiarism-detection tools are rendered ineffective in this context, as AI becomes more capable of human-like text
Detection tools which purport to specifically focus on GenAI detection raise some significant implications for privacy, equity, and data security
Increasingly there has been a recognition that these tools may disproportionally misjudge the work of non-native English writers
these tools are not designed to address complex emotional or mental health concerns. Their guidance may be incomplete or even misleading
This approach is very vulnerable to collusion, copying or outsourcing through the use of contract cheating services or Generative AI.
Programme handbooks must also clearly outline and communicate the permitted use of GenAI by students in learning activities and assessment tasks
If individual modules have further restrictions or permit greater allowances in the use of GenAI, those restrictions or allowances must be stated in the module descriptions in the Blackboard VLE.
In such circumstances, it is the module permissions regarding the use of GenAI which are deemed to be definitive for use in that module.
All students must complete a signed declaration to be submitted with all assessed coursework, declaring that they have read and understood the Library guide on Academic Integrity and Generative AI
Students should familiarise themselves with the Library Guide on Generative AI, which outlines considerations for using and acknowledging the use of Gen AI in academic work.
Any use of generative AI in assessment should be explicitly acknowledged in the work and should comply with the University and departmental guidance on the use of AI.
Any assessments that are generated in whole or part by AI without appropriate acknowledgment and/or referencing shall be considered Unacceptable Academic Practice.
presenting work generated by AI as if it were your own

if it is suspected the work has been obtained from an essay bank or generated through AI software, the Chair of Examination Board may determine that an interview to determine authenticity of work be held

Staff or students are not permitted to upload student assessment, or any identifiable data without explicit written consent, to AI applications for any reason (including attempts to check for AI generated content).
Staff and students will not be permitted to present work completed by AI applications as their own without acknowledgement.
Staff and students should not enter any identifiable information into any AI application.
Users must always ensure the accuracy of results produced by generative AI tools.
The University will enable the use of AI applications in assessment where this is appropriate and relevant to enhance student learning.
Non-compliance with this policy will be reported to the Regulations, Quality and Standards Board.
Formally, this policy will be reviewed at least annually.
using AI to generate material for submission where this is not permitted;
Using automated paraphrasing software.

Generative-Artificial Intelligence detection software will not normally be used in the operation of this procedure, to either evidence allegations of academic misconduct or as a tool in an investigation of academic misconduct.
Instruct students to complete and submit the Generative-Artificial Intelligence Declaration coversheet for all appropriate assessments

Plagiarism: using without acknowledgement another person’s words or ideas and submitting them for assessment as though it were one’s own work. This includes copying materials from the internet, unfair use of generative artificial intelligence software
The Panel of Enquiry must not normally consider information sourced from GenerativeArtificial Intelligence detection software.
Schools must provide students with guidance on any subject- or discipline-specific examples of academic misconduct.
make acknowledgements in submitted work as required by the University and/or their subject or discipline (e.g. to sources, methods, translation, use of generative artificial intelligence software)
Academic integrity is breached if students submit the products of GenAI as their own work without acknowledgement and without authorisation to use GenAI in fulﬁlling the task.
The use of GenAI detection software for the detection or investigation of alleged academic misconduct is not sanctioned by the University.

Students are responsible for ensuring that all submitted work meets the University standards for academic integrity and for avoiding academic misconduct in all its forms including but not limited to the examples listed above: cheating, plagiarism, contract cheating, impersonation, and the unethical use of Gen(AI).
